title: Where the Moon came from
teaches: Three theories that Apollo's samples ruled out, the giant impact that replaced them, and the oxygen puzzle that remains

blocks.text: Before Apollo flew, there were three main ideas about the Moon's origin, and one of the hopes for the samples was that they would decide between them.

**Fission.** In 1879 George Darwin, son of Charles, worked out that tides are slowly pushing the Moon away from the Earth and slowing the Earth's spin. Run that backward and the two were once close together, with the Earth spinning fast. Darwin suggested that a molten, rapidly spinning Earth had flung off a blob that became the Moon. In 1882 the geologist Osmond Fisher proposed that the Pacific Ocean basin was the scar it left behind. **Capture.** The Moon formed elsewhere in the solar system and was caught by Earth's gravity as it passed. **Co-formation.** The Earth and the Moon grew side by side, out of the same cloud of dust and rock around the young Sun, like a double planet.

blocks.caption: Earthrise, photographed by Bill Anders on Apollo 8, 24 December 1968.

blocks.text: Each idea made predictions. Fission predicts a Moon made of Earth's outer layers. Capture predicts a Moon unlike Earth in composition, since it formed somewhere else. Co-formation predicts a Moon made of the same mix as the Earth, including its share of iron.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Fission: a fast-spinning Earth threw off the Moon.
Capture: the Moon formed elsewhere and was caught by Earth's gravity.
Co-formation: Earth and Moon grew side by side from the same material.

blocks.text: The samples and the measurements made around them gave four results, and each theory failed on at least one.

First, the Moon has very little iron. Its average density is 3.34 grams per cubic centimetre, against Earth's 5.51 (lesson D1 explains how Earth's density was measured). Its iron core, detected later from the Moon's gravity and from seismometers the crews left behind, holds only 1 to 2 per cent of its mass, against about 32 per cent for Earth's. Co-formation from the same material should have given the Moon an Earth-like share of iron, so co-formation fails.

Second, the Moon is dry and short of **volatile** elements, ones like sodium, potassium and zinc that evaporate at relatively low temperatures. Lunar rocks contain far less of them than Earth's mantle rocks do. Something heated the Moon's material hot enough to drive them off.

Third, the oxygen in lunar rocks is indistinguishable from Earth's. Oxygen has three stable isotopes (forms of the atom with different masses, lesson 7), and in 1973 the University of Chicago chemist Robert Clayton showed that each body in the solar system carries its own ratio of them, set by where in the young solar system its material came together. Meteorites from Mars, and most other kinds of meteorite, plot as their own groups; lunar rocks sit exactly with Earth's. Capture of a body from elsewhere fails here.

Fourth, fission fails on mechanics. To fling off the Moon, the Earth would have needed to spin once every two and a half hours or so, and the total spin of the Earth and Moon together, which is conserved, is too small for that. The Pacific Ocean floor turned out to be less than 200 million years old (lesson 9), far younger than the Moon.

blocks.caption: Lunar samples are kept in nitrogen-filled cabinets at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, and handled through gloves so that Earth's air and moisture never touch them.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The Moon has a tiny iron core and an average density of 3.34 g/cm³, against Earth's 5.51.
Lunar rocks are depleted in volatile elements and water.
Lunar oxygen isotopes match Earth's, unlike those of Mars and most meteorites.
The Earth-Moon system has too little spin for fission.

blocks.text: In 1975 William Hartmann and Donald Davis at the Planetary Science Institute in Tucson proposed a different event, and in 1976 Alastair Cameron and William Ward at Harvard reached the same idea from the spin. Late in the building of the planets, a body roughly the size of Mars, now often called Theia, struck the young Earth a glancing blow. The impact melted and vaporized much of both bodies' outer layers and threw a disk of hot debris into orbit around the Earth. The Moon gathered out of that disk, probably within a few thousand years or less.

The idea answers each of the four results. By the time of the impact, both bodies had already separated their iron into cores, as lesson D1 shows Earth did. A glancing blow throws out mostly rocky outer layers, while the iron cores merge into the Earth, so the Moon is made of iron-poor rock. Debris that has been vaporized and heated to thousands of degrees loses its volatile elements. An off-centre hit sets the Earth spinning fast, which supplies the spin that fission lacked. And if Theia formed near the Earth, its oxygen could have been similar.

The idea was not taken seriously at first. It was invoking a unique catastrophe, and planetary scientists preferred processes that happen routinely. The turning point was a conference at Kona, Hawaii, in 1984, where the arguments for the other theories were set side by side with the impact. The impact was the only one left standing, and it has been the leading explanation since.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The giant impact hypothesis (Hartmann and Davis 1975, Cameron and Ward 1976): a Mars-sized body struck the young Earth a glancing blow.
The Moon formed from the debris, mostly rocky outer layers, which explains its small core and its lack of volatiles.
The idea became the leading explanation after a 1984 conference at Kona.

blocks.text: As computers grew powerful enough to simulate the impact in detail, from about 2000, they produced a problem. In the simulations that best reproduce the Moon's mass and the Earth's spin, most of the Moon, 60 to 90 per cent, comes from Theia, not from the Earth. If Theia's oxygen differed from Earth's even as much as Mars's does, the Moon should carry a clear trace of that difference. Measurements, by then far more precise, show none: in 2016 Edward Young's group at UCLA found Earth and Moon rocks identical to within a few parts per million.

blocks.caption: Build a Moon from a mixture of the impactor and Earth's mantle. The impactor's oxygen differs from Earth's by the amount you set (Mars's differs by about 0.3 parts per thousand); the green band is what the Apollo samples measure. The small share of the impactor mixed into the Earth itself is ignored.
blocks.task: Find a Moon that matches the samples with a Mars-like impactor

blocks.text: Several explanations are now argued over. Perhaps Theia formed close to the Earth and happened to have almost the same oxygen; certain meteorites, the enstatite chondrites, do match Earth's oxygen closely, showing that material like that existed. Perhaps the impact was far more violent than first thought, enough to vaporize and thoroughly mix both bodies' outer layers into a single spinning cloud of rock vapour, from which Earth and Moon both condensed. Perhaps the young Earth was spinning very fast before the impact, so that more of the Moon came from the Earth itself. Other elements, titanium and tungsten among them, show the same near-perfect match, and any explanation has to account for all of them.

The Apollo samples answered the questions they were collected to answer, and ruled out every theory that existed when they were gathered. The theory that replaced them came from those results, and the samples, measured more precisely half a century later, have now set it a new question.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Simulations suggest most of the Moon came from the impactor, yet Moon and Earth rocks match in oxygen to within a few parts per million.
Proposed answers include an impactor with Earth-like composition, a far more violent impact that mixed everything, and a fast-spinning early Earth.

blocks.caption: Six questions on the Moon's origin
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: Which result counts most strongly against co-formation, the Moon growing beside Earth from the same material?
choices: The Moon has very little iron compared with Earth
items.why: Bodies built from the same mix should share a similar proportion of iron. The Moon's core is 1 to 2 per cent of its mass, Earth's about 32 per cent.

items.ask: Which result counts most strongly against capture?
choices: The Moon's oxygen isotopes match Earth's, while bodies formed elsewhere carry their own ratios
The Moon is moving away from the Earth
The Moon is less dense than the Earth
items.why: Clayton showed each region of the early solar system has its own oxygen fingerprint. A body captured from elsewhere should differ from Earth, and lunar rocks don't.

items.ask: Why does a glancing giant impact produce a Moon with little iron?
choices: Iron had already sunk into both bodies' cores, and a glancing blow throws out mostly rocky outer layers
The heat of the impact turned the iron into rock
Iron is too heavy to be thrown into orbit at any speed
items.why: Both bodies had separated into iron cores and rocky mantles. The cores merged with the Earth, while the debris disk that formed the Moon was mostly mantle rock.

items.ask: Why are lunar rocks short of volatile elements such as sodium and zinc?
choices: The debris that formed the Moon was heated to thousands of degrees, driving them off
The solar wind has stripped them from the Moon's surface
They sank into the Moon's core
items.why: Volatile elements evaporate at relatively low temperatures. The hot, partly vaporized debris disk lost much of them.

items.ask: What is the oxygen puzzle that the giant impact theory still faces?
choices: Simulations make most of the Moon from the impactor, yet the Moon's oxygen matches Earth's within a few parts per million
The Moon has no oxygen at all
Lunar oxygen matches Mars rather than the Earth
items.why: If the impactor's oxygen differed from Earth's as Mars's does, a Moon built mostly from it should show the difference. It doesn't.

items.ask: How are lunar samples stored at the Johnson Space Center, as shown here, and why?
choices: In nitrogen-filled cabinets, handled through gloves, so Earth's air and water never touch them
Frozen in liquid nitrogen, to stop them decaying
In vacuum chambers, because lunar rock burns in air
items.why: Lunar rocks formed with almost no water or oxygen. Keeping them in dry nitrogen preserves the chemistry scientists still measure today.

learned: Before Apollo, fission, capture and co-formation competed to explain the Moon.
The samples showed a Moon poor in iron and volatiles yet matching Earth's oxygen, which ruled out all three.
A glancing impact by a Mars-sized body explains the Moon's small core, dryness and the Earth's spin.
The near-perfect match of Earth and Moon isotopes remains unexplained in detail.
